title: In 126 TESS complex periodic variables, sharp dips are not locked to the broad spot modulation: phases are near random to its minimum, no antipodal pair excess, and dips stay when it moves
abstract: Complex periodic variables (CPVs) are young, rapidly rotating M dwarfs with sharp dips at the rotation period on top of a broad, spot-like modulation. Earlier campaign work showed that the dips keep fixed phases for months, so the material corotates rigidly. We tested which structure sets the dip longitudes. We used the published TESS 2-minute window harmonic models (2018-2026; 10,870 windows, 265 visits, 126 on-target CPVs). For each visit, we fitted a broad part (harmonics 1-2) plus narrow Gaussian dips, and measured each dip phase relative to the broad harmonic-1 minimum. Injections into the same profiles calibrated the tests. (1) For the deepest dip (248 visits, 125 stars), mean cos(2 pi offset) is 0.03 (95%: -0.07 to 0.13); injected aligned dips give 0.85. At most 7-12% of deepest dips sit at the broad minimum, and at most 17-38% at +-0.25 cycle, the nodes of a dipole with its pole at the main spot. A best-measured subset (113 visits) shows a weak preference for the broad minimum (0.16; 0.02 to 0.30). (2) Model-free profile minima show no excess of antipodal pairs, as a simple tilted-dipole torus predicts: excess 5% (-4% to 15%). (3) In 30 visits, the broad minimum drifts by more than 3 errors (0.5% in a fixed-broad null), up to 3e-3 cycles per rotation, but the dips do not follow: errors-in-variables slope -0.02 (-0.22 to 0.10), against 1 for co-motion. Thus, in most CPVs the material is not rooted above the dominant spot longitude, and the structure that holds it is more stable than the spot pattern. Limitations: the broad term can include non-spot light; decompositions of crowded profiles are not unique; one band; visit means smear changes.
